title: Metabolic and Functional Recovery After Intracerebral Hemorrhage Following Structured Hydrogen-Based Infusion Therapy: A Case Report
content: Background:  Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is associated with substantial long-term neurological disability. The clinical role of hydrogen-based nanobubble infusion as an adjunct to rehabilitation remains uncertain. Methods: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension and residual right hemiparesis after left basal ganglia hemorrhage received 29 adjunctive hydrogen–oxygen nanobubble (HHO) infusion sessions beginning approximately three months after stroke onset; intermittent nitric oxide (NO) supplementation was recorded during later sessions. Results: Right upper- and lower-limb strength changed from Medical Research Council (MRC) grade 2/5 to 3/5. Total cholesterol changed from 243 to 138 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol from 169 to 66 mg/dL, serum uric acid from 7.1 to 3.3 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate from 68 to 42 mm/h. After 19 sessions, follow-up computed tomography showed disappearance of the initial hematoma and residual chronic cerebral changes without new hemorrhage. A transient low-grade fever was reported during early sessions. Conclusions: These observations document a favorable clinical course during combined standard care, rehabilitation, and adjunctive treatment. A single uncontrolled case cannot determine whether HHO–NO contributed to recovery, hematoma clearance, metabolic changes, or treatment safety. Standardized formulation characterization and controlled clinical investigation are warranted.
